dek_candidates: What the DRHP discloses about 20 Microns Nano Minerals' business, offer, financials and risks — sourced to the filing, page by page.
A specialty chemicals processor with ₹34.25 crore in restated assets, a 99.76% promoter holding and a new plant planned at Waghodia. Here is what the filing says, and what it leaves out.
design_notes: Every restated statement figure is in ₹ lakh; convert to ₹ crore at ÷100, show both in the table, and never estimate a figure the digest does not carry.

Where a number is absent — issue size, price band, revenue, EBITDA, debt, peer multiples — write 'not disclosed in the excerpted pages' and move on; do not soften it into 'not available' or infer a value.
Explain-then-ground in every section: the plain claim first, the specific number or disclosure second, the page citation third — citations are evidence, never the sentence itself.
The business model is the story: purchase-order selling, a concentrated customer book, and a distribution network owned by the promoter company. Keep returning to that triangle.

The financials section must run the full six periods in prose and in the table, not two sentences. The FY2017 operating cash outflow and the six-month versus full-year comparison are the two points a reader needs to leave with.
No verdict, no price talk, no listing-gain or subscription language anywhere in the draft.

beats.beat: The company describes itself as engaged in processing and selling specialty chemicals across four families — Functional Additives (FA) and Chemically Modified Minerals (CMM), plus Soft Minerals (SM) and Hard Minerals (HM). 'Processing' is the operative verb: it buys mineral feedstock and chemical inputs, treats them, and sells the treated output to industrial buyers.

How contracts are actually won: not through long-term supply agreements. The filing discloses that the company has not entered into any long-term or definitive agreements with its customers and instead relies on purchase orders to govern volume, pricing and other terms of sale. That is a month-to-month or order-to-order business, which is why the same risk appears high in the filing's own risk list.

Route to market: the company states it has a long-term arrangement with its corporate promoter to market and sell its products through the promoter's network, and lists 'support of our holding company' as a stated strength and a source of 'substantial synergies' with 20 Microns Limited. For a reader, this means a large share of the company's selling infrastructure belongs to a related entity, not to the company itself.

Customer concentration, quantified: the top 10 customers accounted for around 59% of revenue from operations in FY2017, 57% in FY2016 and 59% in FY2015. Roughly three-fifths of the business sits with ten buyers, and those buyers have no long-term contracts.
Exports: over the past five years the company says it achieved exports of ₹1,068.18 lakh, shipping to Nigeria, Saudi Arabia and Sri Lanka. Three named markets, no disclosed split by country.

The six strengths the filing claims for itself, grouped rather than listed: a diversified product portfolio, diversified user industries, import substitution (supplying domestically what would otherwise be imported), support of its holding company, product innovation with continuous R&D, and a strong management team. Read as a set, they describe a niche processor competing against imports rather than a branded manufacturer.

What the excerpted pages do not give about the business: revenue split by product segment or by customer industry, plant count, installed capacity, utilisation, headcount and R&D spend. The piece should say these are not disclosed in the excerpted pages rather than infer them.

business.heading: What the company does, and how the money reaches it
business.purpose: Explain the product lines, the route to market, and the two structural facts that shape both: promoter-run distribution and a concentrated customer base.

beats.beat: A conversion note first, because the reader will meet both units: the restated statements are presented in ₹ lakh. One crore is one hundred lakh, so ₹149.58 lakh is ₹1.50 crore.

Profit after tax across all six reported periods, in the filing's own lakh figures: FY2013 ₹(27.40) lakh, FY2014 ₹(12.17) lakh, FY2015 ₹149.58 lakh, FY2016 ₹90.18 lakh, FY2017 ₹174.82 lakh, and the six months ended September 30, 2017 ₹132.75 lakh. In ₹ crore: (0.27), (0.12), 1.50, 0.90, 1.75 and 1.33.

What that pattern means, plainly: two loss years, then a switch to profit in FY2015. Profit fell by roughly 40% the next year, rose sharply in FY2017, and the first half of FY2018 alone produced most of FY2017's full-year profit — which is flattering to the half-year column and worth saying out loud, since a six-month figure is not comparable with a full year.
Earnings per share, same six periods: ₹(0.45), ₹(0.20), ₹2.47, ₹1.46, ₹2.43 and ₹1.48. The FY2015 EPS of ₹2.47 is the highest in the series; the FY2017 figure of ₹2.43 is close behind it.

Cash generated by operations, the line that matters most for a capital-hungry processor: FY2013 ₹200.97 lakh, FY2014 ₹127.73 lakh, FY2015 ₹422.36 lakh, FY2016 ₹802.59 lakh, FY2017 ₹(349.75) lakh, and the six months to September 30, 2017 ₹124.86 lakh. In ₹ crore: 2.01, 1.28, 4.22, 8.03, (3.50) and 1.25. The FY2017 outflow is the one the filing itself flags in its risk list.

What the cash flow swing suggests: operating cash rose for two years, then flipped to a ₹3.50 crore outflow in FY2017 and back to a ₹1.25 crore inflow in the half year. A business that can generate ₹8.03 crore in a good year and lose ₹3.50 crore the next is a working-capital-sensitive business — inventory and receivables in a commodity-linked trade, as the underlying cash flow statement would show.

Restated total assets across the same six periods: ₹3,018.66 lakh in FY2013 (₹30.19 crore), ₹2,679.38 lakh in FY2014 (₹26.79 crore), ₹2,592.53 lakh in FY2015 (₹25.93 crore), ₹2,767.21 lakh in FY2016 (₹27.67 crore), ₹3,273.96 lakh in FY2017 (₹32.74 crore) and ₹3,424.96 lakh at September 30, 2017 (₹34.25 crore). The balance sheet shrank for two years before it grew.

Share capital, which fixes the per-share denominators: authorised share capital of ₹2,000.00 lakh, being 20,00,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, and issued, subscribed and paid-up capital of ₹897.00 lakh, being 89,70,000 equity shares of ₹10 each, as at September 30, 2017.
Off-balance-sheet: contingent liabilities and commitments, to the extent not provided for, aggregated ₹29.11 lakh as at September 30, 2017, per the notes to the restated financial information.

What the excerpted statements do not carry, and must be labelled as not disclosed: the revenue from operations line for any period, any EBITDA measure, and the borrowing or debt figure. The filing does disclose that unsecured loans taken by the company, its promoters, group companies or associates can be recalled at any time, and that loan agreements carry restrictive covenants — but not the amounts.

financials.purpose: Walk the reader through the restated profit, cash flow, assets and share capital across every reported period, in ₹ crore, and explain what the pattern actually shows.

beats.beat: The promoters of the company are named individually and as a company: Mr. Chandresh S. Parikh, Mr. Atil C. Parikh, Mr. Rajesh C. Parikh and 20 Microns Limited. Three individuals and the listed parent entity.

How concentrated the ownership is: the promoters hold, in aggregate, 89,48,270 equity shares — 99.76% of the pre-issue paid-up equity share capital. The promoter group excluding the promoters holds a further 21,510 shares, or 0.24%. Between them, the pre-issue register is effectively entirely insider-owned; there is no pre-issue public float of any size.

Related-party transactions are not incidental here. The filing states the company has in the past entered into related party transactions and may continue to do so, with no assurance that they will not adversely affect the company's financial condition and results of operations, and directs readers to Accounting Standard 18 disclosures in the financial statements covering the last five financial years and the six months ended September 30, 2017. Combined with sales routed through the corporate promoter's network, related-party dealings sit at the centre of how this business earns revenue.

Registrar of Companies compliance history: the filing discloses past instances of non-filings, incorrect filings or delays in filing statutory forms with the RoC, in certain cases subsequently filed with additional fees as specified by the RoC.

Licensing: the company has not yet obtained certain statutory and regulatory licences, registrations and approvals required to operate its manufacturing facility at Plot 9-10, GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara, Gujarat, and it says it cannot assure that it will not be penalised for such non-compliance.

Assets the company does not own: the premises housing the manufacturing facilities at Plot 347, GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara, Gujarat and Plot 104/3, Thenkasi Road, Pathur Village, Alangulam, Tirunelveli, Tamil Nadu, plus the administrative offices in Bhuj and Udaipur, are not owned by the company. It also states it has not yet obtained registration for its corporate logo.

Litigation, stated at the level of detail the excerpted pages allow: the company, its promoters, its group company and its directors are parties to certain legal proceedings, and an adverse decision could materially affect business, results of operations and financial condition. The quantum is not given in the excerpted pages.

beats.beat: Where this company sits: specialty chemicals excluding agrochemicals and dyestuffs accounted for about 17% of the Indian chemicals industry, at roughly ₹1,000 billion, against a total Indian chemicals industry (excluding pharmaceuticals and fertilisers) of ₹5,800–6,200 billion in fiscal 2017. Specialty chemicals is the smaller, higher-value slice of a very large industry.

Growth: the specialty chemicals segment grew at 10–12% CAGR from fiscal 2014 to 2017, and CRISIL Research forecasts 12–14% CAGR going forward, taking the segment to ₹1,443 billion. Two numbers from the same page that frame the opportunity.

The sub-segments grow at different speeds, and this matters because the filing does not say which ones the company serves. Textile chemicals 12% CAGR; surfactants 13%; polymer additives 10%; construction chemicals 15%; water chemicals 15%; personal care ingredients 15%; flavours and fragrances 12%.

Industry structure: highly fragmented, with SMEs holding 70–75% market share, while only a few Indian players have the scale or capability to compete with global giants on product development and innovation. This is the filing describing a crowded low end and a thin high end — and the company is a small player in that crowd.

Demand drivers as the filing frames them: rising intensity of consumption, improved consumption standards, and end-use demand tied to a middle class the filing says could reach 148 million households by 2030.

Policy tailwinds: a Draft National Chemical Policy aimed at lifting the chemicals sector's share of GDP, industrial licensing scrapped for most chemicals outside a short hazardous list, and FDI permitted up to 100% in the sector.

A global factor the filing leans on: China, a major commodity chemicals player, has focused less on specialty chemicals because of the segment's low-volume, high-value nature, and stricter environmental regulations introduced there in 2015 hit its chemical manufacturing output. That is presented as an opening for Indian suppliers.

Downstream demand, named: polymer demand forecast at 9–10% CAGR between fiscals 2017 and 2020; plastic products at 11–13%; the domestic paints industry at ₹401 billion in fiscal 2017; and the organised cosmetics and toiletries market at ₹430–460 billion.

Headwinds the filing names: the chemicals industry has run a trade deficit every year from 2012-13 to 2016-17, with imports growing faster than exports (6.4% CAGR against 6%); exports to Europe face the REACH regulatory regime; and GST replaced the earlier indirect tax stack from July 1, 2017. The four approved Petroleum, Chemicals and Petrochemicals Investment Regions — Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Odisha, with about ₹9 trillion of proposed investment — are the infrastructure counterweight.

Macro backdrop in one beat: India's GDP grew 7.1% in fiscal 2017, private consumption is the largest contributor to GDP at 58%, and urban population was about 31% in 2011 with the filing projecting 36% by 2020.
Note for the reader: the excerpted pages name no competitor of the company by name. Competition is described as a category ('global giants', SMEs), not as a list of rivals.

beats.beat: Plain orientation: 20 Microns Nano Minerals processes and sells specialty chemicals — functional additives and chemically modified minerals — and also processes soft minerals and hard minerals. Specialty chemicals are inputs sold to other manufacturers rather than products a consumer buys directly, so the customer is a factory, not a shopper.
Name the four product families the filing uses, in the filing's own terms: Functional Additives (FA), Chemically Modified Minerals (CMM), Soft Minerals (SM) and Hard Minerals (HM).

The single most unusual thing about the business: it does not build its own sales force so much as plug into its corporate promoter's. The company states it has a long-term arrangement with its corporate promoter — 20 Microns Limited — to market and sell its products through that promoter's network, and separately lists 'support of our holding company' as one of its strengths.

Scale, in the numbers the filing gives: restated total assets of ₹3,424.96 lakh (₹34.25 crore) as at September 30, 2017, and restated profit after tax of ₹174.82 lakh (₹1.75 crore) for the year ended March 31, 2017. The restated statements are presented in ₹ lakh throughout.

What the money is for: capital expenditure on a new manufacturing facility at Plot 336, GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara, Gujarat, plus general corporate purposes, plus creating a public trading market by listing on the SME platform of NSE (NSE EMERGE) to raise visibility and brand.

Framing sentence for the piece: this is a read of the DRHP, not a view on whether to apply. Several things a reader would normally expect in an IPO story — the issue size, the price band, the revenue line — are not in the excerpted pages, and the piece will say so rather than fill them in.

intro.purpose: Orient a reader who has never heard of this company: what it makes, who it sells through, how big it is, and what the issue is for.

beats.beat: Define the two halves of an Indian public issue before going further: a fresh issue creates new shares and the money goes to the company; an offer for sale sells existing shares held by an existing owner and the money goes to that seller, not the company. Most issues mix the two.

First named object of the issue: to fund capital expenditure for setting up a new manufacturing facility at Plot 336, GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara, Gujarat. This is the concrete purpose for which fresh capital would be used — a new plant at a named plot in a named industrial estate.

Second object: general corporate purposes. Third, and distinct in kind: creating a public trading market for the equity shares by listing them on the SME Platform of NSE (NSE EMERGE) to enhance visibility and brand.
The intermediaries named in the filing: Vivro Financial Services Private Limited as lead manager and Link Intime India Private Limited as registrar.

What the excerpted pages do not disclose, and must be stated as not disclosed: the issue size, the split between fresh issue and offer for sale, the identity of any selling shareholder, the price band, the lot size and the bid dates. Nothing in the digest supports an estimate of any of these, and the piece should not attempt one.

beats.beat: Risk 1 — no long-term customer contracts, on top of a concentrated book. The company relies on purchase orders rather than definitive agreements to set volume, pricing and other sale terms, and its top 10 customers accounted for around 59% of FY2017 revenue, 57% in FY2016 and 59% in FY2015. Put together: roughly three-fifths of revenue rests with ten buyers who have made no contractual commitment beyond the next order.

Risk 2 — a plant without full regulatory clearance. The company discloses that it has not obtained certain statutory and regulatory licences, registrations and approvals required to operate the manufacturing facility at Plot 9-10, GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara, and that it cannot assure it will not be penalised for the non-compliance. A licence the company operates without is a licence a regulator can act on.

Risk 3 — operating cash flow turned negative in FY2017. The filing states as a risk that the company had negative cash flows in previous financial years per the restated financial statements; the restated cash flow statement shows a ₹(349.75) lakh, or ₹(3.50) crore, net outflow from operating activities for the year ended March 31, 2017, after four consecutive years of inflows. Sustained negative operating cash flow would constrain growth without external funding.

Risk 4 — the company sells through its promoter. It markets and sells products through the network of its corporate promoter, 20 Microns Limited, under a long-term arrangement, and derives what it calls substantial synergies from that promoter. It also discloses that related party transactions may continue and that there is no assurance they will not adversely affect its financial condition and results of operations. Revenues and related-party dealings run through the same channel.

Risk 5 — litigation against the company and the people who run it. The filing states that the company, its promoters, its group company and its directors are parties to certain legal proceedings, and that an adverse decision could have a material adverse effect on business, results of operations and financial condition. The excerpted pages do not quantify the claims.

One closing note that belongs in the sidebar rather than in the five: the company also discloses that it has no long-term agreements with raw material suppliers, that it is exposed to foreign currency fluctuations, that it faces product liability claims on quality and defects, and that its loan agreements carry restrictive covenants with unconditional lender rights. These are real, but secondary to the five above.

risks.heading: The five risks that matter
risks.purpose: Pick the five most company-specific risks the filing discloses, explain each in plain words, and stop at five.

beats.beat: The only earnings input the excerpted pages provide is the restated earnings per share series — ₹(0.45), ₹(0.20), ₹2.47, ₹1.46, ₹2.43 and ₹1.48 across FY2013 to the six months ended September 30, 2017. Whatever a reader thinks the multiple should be, the denominator is this line.

The share count that turns earnings into a per-share base: 89,70,000 equity shares of ₹10 each issued, subscribed and paid-up as at September 30, 2017, against authorised capital of 20,00,00,000 such shares.

Why no peer table and no implied price range appear in this report: the excerpted pages do not carry a peer comparison with named peers, their P/E, EPS, NAV or RoNW, and they do not carry a price band for the issue. Without a price band there is no issue price to divide by EPS, and without peer multiples there is no comparable to anchor an implied range to. The omission is the finding.
